title: CCTV Weekly Script 23/02/24
text:
— This is the weekly script of CNBC's news report for China's CCTV on February 23, 2024.
Jensen Huang
People of the Week begins with the CEO of NVIDIA Jensen Huang who currently dominates the headlines of many financial media.
About a year ago, we reported Jensen Huang describing the generative AI as reaching a turning point. But this week, Huang changed his wording, stating that generative AI has reached a tipping point. From a turning point to a tipping point, riding the favorable winds, NVIDIA has been soaring. The market's attention on NVIDIA began early in the week. Before the financial report was released, Goldman Sachs boldly stated that NVIDIA is currently the most important stock on Earth. The results of the financial report would impact the tech stocks and the future market trend. NVIDIA lived up to expectations, igniting trading enthusiasm in the U.S. stock market, once again drawing attention to the rapid development of generative AI.
Notably, due to the high price of NVIDIA, some analysts believed that meeting or slightly exceeding expectations would not satisfy the market. Therefore, some traders sold off before the financial report to lock in profits. As a result, NVIDIA experienced a roughly 4% decline in a single day this week before witnessing an almost 90-degree upward surge.
The current market debate revolves around whether NVIDIA's high valuation is justified, but there are also steadfast followers. Jim Cramer, a renowned market commentator on CNBC, has been bullish on NVIDIA since 2017. Cramer even likened Jensen Huang to the Taylor Swift of CEOs, believing that they have been steadfast in their chosen careers, consistently making tangible progress. Cramer believes that Huang "is creating, singlehandedly, an industrial revolution," to change the world.
Masayoshi Son
Now NVIDIA dominates the major share of the AI chip market, but there is an investor who wants to join this competition, and that is Masayoshi Son, the founder of SoftBank Group.
In recent years, Son has repeatedly predicted in his speeches that Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) is the future of human civilization. AGI refers to an artificial intelligence system that can perform tasks requiring any level of intelligence equal to or surpassing that of humans. Bloomberg reported this week, citing sources, that Son is seeking to raise $100 billion to establish an AI chip company with the aim of challenging NVIDIA. If successful, this investment will surpass Microsoft's $10 billion investment in OpenAI, becoming the largest investment in the field of AI since the birth of ChatGPT.
In the past few years, Son suffered losses in his investments in the tech industry but has recently gained rewards with the chip design company Arm. It is reported that Son is considering a joint venture to establish this AI chip company, with SoftBank providing $30 billion, and the remaining approximately $70 billion possibly coming from the Middle East. And there was an interesting story here – Son and Huang almost created the largest merger in the semiconductor industry. NVIDIA had once planned to acquire Arm for a valuation as high as $66 billion, but the deal ultimately fell through. Unexpectedly, after twists and turns, Son and Huang may soon become direct competitors in the AI chip battlefield.
Sam Altman
The market's enthusiasm for AI chips can be traced back to the chatbot ChatGPT, which triggered all these developments. Next, let's focus on the father of ChatGPT, Sam Altman.
The initially released chatbot by OpenAI gave the public a glimpse of the potential of generative AI. Recently, its text-to-video model, Sora, can be considered a complete breakthrough. Although Sora has not been made available to the public and is still undergoing red-teaming, Altman knows how to party. On social media, he asked users to leave descriptions for Sora to generate videos, assuring them not to worry about making requests too detailed or difficult. Later he released videos generated based on user descriptions, sparking discussions. Now, not only the tech and finance circles but also industries such as advertising, media, and content production are discussing Sora. Some envision future opportunities, while others anticipate significant changes in the industry.
In fact, Sora is not the first text-to-video model. Before it, startups like Runway and Pika had already started a wave of enthusiasm for AI video applications. However, Sora has generated such significant attention this time because it has achieved incredible video quality and duration breakthroughs. Some experts even believe that Sora has laid the foundation for Artificial General Intelligence.
We highlighted a few names who have emerged and surfed in the wave of generative AI, but this is just the beginning. Who will be the next to drive the technological revolution in the future? Please stay tuned!

title: What’s the future of advertising? Ask Sora - ET BrandEquity
text:

What’s the future of advertising? Ask Sora
Sora, a new service from OpenAI that produces one-minute videos in response to a textual prompt, isn’t yet available to the public. But it’s already got content creators fretting about their jobs. What are the future economic consequences of this development – couldit put film-making or advertisers out of business? Not just yet but the introduction of Sora is more evidence that AI, particularly images, is progressing more rapidly than text.
Sora, a new service from OpenAI that produces one-minute videos in response to a text prompt, isn’t yet available to the public. But the videos it has released are striking for their vividness, their detail and, if this is the correct term for an AI, their imagination. Consider the future economic consequences of this development.
Threat to film-making business?
First, Sora is unlikely to put film-making or the industry itself out of business. Eventually, these videos will get much longer, but it remains to be seen how well AI can construct long story arcs into a commercially appealing package. Cost is an additional consideration.
The more clear and present danger to the business is that would-be viewers might start making their own short videos rather than watching television. “Show my pet dog Fido flying to Mars and building a space colony there” is perhaps more fun than many TV shows.
Sora and comparable services will lead to a proliferation of short educational videos, internal corporate training videos and just plain fooling around. Sora probably will be good for short video services. It is not hard to imagine services that splice your Sora-constructed videos into your productions.
Perhaps the most significant short-run use of these videos will be for advertising — especially internet advertising. Again, there is the question of how to integrate narrative, but the costs of creating new ads is likely to fall.
More fun and creative
More advertising may sound like a mixed blessing. But ads will almost certainly be more fun and creative than they are now. Watching ads may become its own aesthetic avocation, as is already the case in the US for Super Bowl ads. These ads also might be targeted, rather than serving a mass audience. If your internet history suggests you are interested in unidentified ariel phenomena, for example, perhaps you will see ads with aliens telling you which soap to buy.

There is the notion that Sora has been trained on “synthetic data”, for example, which in this context means other videos created by AIs, rather than videos of real life. To the extent that is true, future AI progress will be to some extent liberated from constraints of data. AIs will be in essence able to teach themselves, which would accelerate AI progress even more.
Sora is yet more evidence that, in AI, progress in images is proceeding more rapidly than progress in text. GPT-4 has now been out for well over a year, and it remains to be seen how much better its successors will be. In that same period of time, image and video production has made amazing strides. It was not so long ago that people used to complain that AI image services could not portray human hands convincingly.

To the extent that is true, future AI progress will be to some extent liberated from constraints of data. AIs will be in essence able to teach themselves, which would accelerate AI progress even more.
Sora is yet more evidence that, in AI, progress in images is proceeding more rapidly than progress in text. GPT-4 has now been out for well over a year, and it remains to be seen how much better its successors will be. In that same period of time, image and video production has made amazing strides. It was not so long ago that people used to complain that AI image services could not portray human hands convincingly.
If progress in images continues to outpace progress in text, then maybe that old saying has it backwards: A word is worth 1,000 pictures. Or, to put another way, words are more truly “human” than images.

"As we enter a new era based on artificial intelligence, we believe this is the best time to articulate principles that will govern how we will operate our AI datacenter infrastructure and other important AI assets around the world," Smith said in a speech to be delivered at the Mobile World Congress in Barcelona.

title: Council Post: AI In Branding: Where Efficiency And Creativity Collide
text:
Founding Partner @ Wunderdogs, award-winning branding agency and digital studio for high-growth companies and venture capital firms.
Advancements in artificial intelligence, most notably in generative image technology and large language models, have sparked both excitement and a wave of apprehension across numerous industries. Critical observers express concern over AI’s impact on human creativity and fear a future where a wide range of jobs might become obsolete. This type of backlash, however, is not unprecedented. Groundbreaking technologies have historically provoked unease about their implications for humanity's creativity and intellect.
For instance, information overload was deemed "confusing and harmful" to the human mind hundreds of years ago, when Swiss scientist Conrad Gessner condemned the printing press. He argued that the sheer volume of books would create chaos. Similarly, when "talkies" replaced silent films, many directors and critics worried they would dampen invention and creativity in cinema, with some even declaring that "sound is the death of film." The rise of AI therefore fits into this broader historical narrative of backlash against disruptive technology.
In branding and marketing, the advent of AI has ignited some intense discussions. The past year alone has witnessed a surge in AI tools aimed at revolutionizing branding practices. Yet the questions remain: Does AI truly enhance the creative process, or does it signal the end of human creativity in these fields? Or maybe, like always, the answer is somewhere in the middle?
The Mixed Bag Of Emergent AI Tools
Since the public release of ChatGPT, DALL-E and Midjourney just over a year ago, the market has been inundated with products claiming to streamline the branding and marketing process. These products range from apps that generate unique color palettes for brands and websites, to those that create logos based on a brand’s name, industry and style preferences. Other tools can generate complete presentations, including both content and design, with minimal input from the user. Some AI tools even claim the ability to analyze consumer behavior and emotions to suggest branding strategies. These emerging tools all claim that they will make a significant impact on the branding and marketing landscape. The pros they list often include saving time and resources and helping smaller companies and startups bootstrap their branding and marketing efforts instead of hiring agencies or freelance professionals.
However, the effectiveness of these AI tools is a topic of ongoing debate. Often, the output from these tools appears generic, lacking the nuanced understanding of a brand's core values that a human designer or brand strategist inherently possesses. While these tools can process data and follow algorithms to create outputs that fit broadly into the current design landscape, my team has found through experimenting with them that they frequently miss the mark in capturing the subtle emotional and psychological elements crucial in effective branding. Critics fear that an overreliance on these types of AI tools could lead to a homogenized and impersonal branding landscape, in which brands fail to resonate with both brand values and consumer interests.
Effective Uses Of AI In Branding
Despite some clear limitations, AI's versatility makes it a valuable asset across various phases of branding—from initial strategy formulation to creative development and marketing execution.
During the strategy phase:
• Data analysis: Long a staple in market research, AI has made data analysis more accessible. Even smaller teams without extensive resources can now access insights into market trends, consumer behavior and brand performance. This allows for more informed decision making and more data-driven approaches to both branding and marketing.
• Predictive analytics: By analyzing historical data and patterns, AI can make predictions about future trends and consumer behavior. This may help brands find unexpected ways to stay ahead of the curve. It’s important to remember, however, that AI is not an all-seeing eye and, as the saying goes, past performance does not guarantee future results. These types of analytics are useful when used in combination with other strategies.
During creative development:
• Brainstorming and inspiration: AI can serve as an excellent tool for generating initial ideas or helping creatives get unstuck. A large part of the creative process involves generating as many ideas as possible to land on a handful that you can develop further. AI’s highly randomized approaches to images and language can help generate vast pools of ideas, of which most will be discarded but some can spark human creativity.
• Proofreading and editing: Getting an extra pair of eyes (or two) on content and copy is paramount to maintain clarity and ensure that brand tone is consistent. AI can act as a proofreader and editor, checking grammar and suggesting improvements for tone or clarity.
For performance marketing:
• Benchmarking: Since many large language models are now plugged into the internet and have the benefit of up-to-date information, AI can efficiently compare a brand’s strategies and performance against competitors. This is a quick and easy way to gain valuable insights into market positioning and potential areas for improvement, which can influence the day-to-day execution of marketing campaigns.
• Personalization: AI can analyze vast amounts of data about individual customers, allowing brands to create personalized experiences and tailor their messaging to specific audiences. When employing this functionality, however, it’s important to make sure that the data you use is ethically and transparently sourced.
None of these applications fully replace human input and insight, but they can streamline processes. Employing AI tools can make branding efforts more efficient and data-driven, while allowing creatives and strategists to focus on innovative approaches that resonate with the audience and the brand’s emotional core.
The Future Of Branding: Balancing AI With Human Creativity
Once a disruptive technology emerges, it often becomes an integral part of society, shaping our daily lives and transforming industries. AI in branding is no exception. But I firmly believe that the future of branding lies not in choosing between AI and human creativity, but in harnessing the synergy between the two.
At my agency, we’ve been using AI-enabled tools to speed up established processes, such as proofreading, and to expand our horizons when generating new ideas. With a few clients, we’ve also used generative imagery in broader brand contexts where it fits the brand’s vision and strategy. We are excited to experiment with new AI tools as they emerge.
Embracing AI tools that complement human creativity can lead to the development of more impactful brand strategies and identities. In this new era, the fusion of AI's efficiency and the emotional depth of human creativity will define the most successful branding narratives.

title: Council Post: AI Takes Over Davos: The Promise, The Risk And The Way Forward
text:
Phil Hall is Chief Growth Officer at LXT, an emerging leader in global AI training data that powers intelligent technology.
As global politicians and business executives recently took to the stage at The World Economic Forum, focal points of discussion included conflicts in Eastern Europe and the Middle East, the ongoing climate crisis and perhaps unsurprisingly, artificial intelligence (AI).
It seems that the AI conversation is shifting focus from excitement about its potential to perceived risks and ways to make it more trustworthy moving forward.
There is an acknowledgment that this powerful technology, alongside its vast promise, has the potential to cause "misinformation, displace jobs and widen the economic gap between wealthy and poor nations." This has sparked a global debate of increasing urgency amongst technology company executives and global government leaders regarding how to balance fast-moving innovation with policy and regulations that will help to set boundaries and ensure the technology’s safe and productive evolution.
So, how did we get here, what does the way forward look like, and will regulation stifle innovation or stimulate it?
Today's Policies And Regulations
The sheer power of ChatGPT and other generative AI applications has put the world on notice and created unease amongst elected officials and business leaders alike. In response, we are seeing a drive towards global regulations coming from Western governments that want to benefit the companies within their borders, while India, South America and the Global South seem to be looking at the technology’s potential to drive economic prosperity.
The forum’s AI Governance Alliance released its comments on AI policy at the event, but it is clear that global leaders are approaching regulation with differing goals and areas of focus—from the Biden Administration's Executive Order on AI that requires developers of the most powerful AI systems to share safety test results and other critical information with the U.S. government to European leaders' recent deal on the EU AI Act which imposes specific obligations on the providers and deployers of AI systems in relation to testing, documentation, transparency and notification.
With these new policies and regulations will come new processes intended to support innovation without compromising accurate, ethical and trustworthy results that will move the technology forward. The hope is that while there may be some friction and tension between these forces, companies, governments and the industry as a whole will find synergy between the two. This would be a boon for the future of trust in AI and a potential tipping point in its meaningful adoption.
Historically, regulation has played a dual role in many important industries, acting both as a catalyst to innovation and a barrier. The automotive, finance and telecommunications industries come to mind, where breakthroughs have been made alongside the establishment of standards that have had a massive impact on quality of life. Seatbelts and electric cars are two striking examples, along with greater choice in general and quality products and services across many markets.
Synergy, Accuracy And Adoption
Let us first take a look at specifically how the two forces of innovation and regulation can provide synergies and then consider how companies can use their own internal resources, expertise, workforce and user bases to ensure accuracy and advance adoption.
Across many industries, regulations have accelerated innovation by setting standards that require new approaches. As in the earlier reference, both stringent safety and environmental regulations led to significant advancements that resulted in today’s seat belts, airbags and electric cars.
Regulations can also spark innovation by creating a stable and predictable environment in which to work, encouraging investment and research in new technologies that will meet these expectations. For example, the European Union’s wide-reaching General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) has led to creative solutions to privacy and data protection in the newly defined landscape.
To ensure accuracy and compliance with new policies and regulations, organizations will have to invest in the right resources. At the top of the list would be the inputs that will ensure that AI applications adequately represent the real world and uphold the criteria outlined in regulations. This would include both high-quality data to train new systems and human feedback to ensure its accuracy.
In Conclusion
New technologies will assist workers at first, much as ChatGPT and other generative AI applications do today, then likely run on autopilot, closely monitored by humans to ensure accuracy and, finally, autonomously—with confidence that the technology will work with accuracy and remain in compliance.
At the end of the day, trust will be the cornerstone of AI adoption. I believe it will be the force that drives the industry forward in many new directions we cannot even imagine yet. With the right mix of innovation, regulation and resources, the way forward looks bright.

title: Council Post: How AI Will Spur The Democratization Of Technology In 2024
text:
Ed Macosky, Chief Product and Technology Officer at Boomi, a leading provider of cloud-based integration platform as a service (iPaaS).
With the artificial intelligence market set to reach nearly $2 trillion by 2030, it’s no secret that the explosion of AI has sparked a remarkable technological shift. Companies looking to participate in the AI race are now scrambling to take advantage of AI systems and incorporate the technology into products and workflows.
However, enterprises face a twofold challenge: adequately integrating AI technology into business processes while ensuring they stay competitive in the market. The AI race has prompted even greater innovation opportunities and potential to drive technological democratization across organizations for both technical and non-technical staff—particularly as enterprises face a scarcity of IT talent.
As AI continues to evolve in the year ahead, businesses must begin fostering a resilient, future-proof foundation to empower teams to take full advantage of AI’s capabilities. This will, in turn, promote enhanced organizational success, competitiveness and creativity in the long run.
Embracing AI To Fuel Collaboration
AI’s impact has evolved notably over the past year and will only continue to accelerate. For enterprises, AI has helped foster collaboration by streamlining existing processes. This has freed up teams and resources to generate better business results and increase business competitiveness. Moreover, AI can act as both a traditional IT assistant and a resource to businesses as they develop a product from ideation to deployment.
Even now, teams are proactively incorporating AI copilots and other technology into workflows and DevOps processes, integrating AI technologies into their code review and writing practices. In this way, the integration of AI is bringing teams—especially software engineering teams—closer together as they identify ways to enhance their overall approach and performance. AI’s ability to promote collaboration benefits enterprises by helping engineering teams put their heads together to think more innovatively about how they can streamline certain processes within their organizations, including use for pilots, proof of concepts (POCs) and testing.
While the work of developer and engineering teams has previously been largely confined to the backend, IT leaders are stepping even further into roles as critical advisors, being more involved in business discussions and company-wide tech trainings as opposed to simply meeting technology needs.
With this increased cross-organizational involvement and collaboration, companies that employ AI for automation, prototyping and testing will need to align on AI strategies for both technical and non-technical staff. This initiative will empower non-developers to innovate more frequently and, as a result, drastically decrease the time required for new project developments. With resilient AI frameworks, non-technical employees will acquire the tools needed to take on tasks typically reserved for technical staff, encouraging the development of creative approaches to generate impactful business results.
Integrating AI Into Business Operations
It’s clear that integrating AI into business processes will drive technological democratization across levels as enterprises grapple with a limited supply of IT talent. However, not many business leaders are confident about how to take that first step. Considering the enduring relevance of AI, organizations must focus on establishing a pragmatic framework to harness AI’s advantages over the long term. Developing this foundation must ultimately be geared toward enhancing business value by streamlining processes, creating innovative products and services and providing compelling user experiences.
While easy-to-use solutions such as low-code technologies have emerged as resources to solve the IT skills gap, an intentional engagement with AI will enable both technical and non-technical staff to build and deploy initiatives while addressing resource scarcity. The resource investment needed for infrastructure maintenance and technical training is usually high, which can impede a business’ ability to adapt quickly and stay ahead of the competition.
These resource hurdles can look especially pronounced during challenging macroeconomic climates and an increasingly competitive landscape. The ability to swiftly and effectively reskill non-technical staff is essential to build organizational resilience. In turn, deliberately implemented AI automation will help businesses reduce the resources needed for IT maintenance, as well as the amount of technical expertise required to build and develop software.
AI In 2024 And Beyond
AI has fundamentally transformed the business landscape by offering a powerful tool to address myriad business functions, and stakeholders have a renewed challenge to ascertain how to effectively use AI to keep up alongside their competitors’ same efforts.
Ultimately, attempts to integrate AI must serve a broader, strategic purpose to drive the competitive outcomes that business leaders desire. The enthusiasm around AI and its rapid technological progression has prompted leaders to move quickly toward implementing AI solutions into their business processes. But despite swift and cutting-edge progress, it is critical for businesses to approach the implementation of AI automation with deliberateness to ensure the longevity of their digital transformation efforts.
Though it is tempting to see all progress as good progress, practical frameworks that promote steady, effective engagement with AI are what will fortify the durability of an enterprise's AI integration strategy in the long run. A future-proof approach, with consideration for how AI will continue to change and mature, is what will unlock transformational business outcomes in the years ahead.
As AI continues to take center stage, enterprises must not only engage with AI but do so promptly. As a result, businesses will empower their teams to collaborate more effectively, and non-technical staff who lack an extensive IT background will unlock the ability to take on more technical tasks with low-code options. The democratization of technology for enterprises in 2024 and beyond, fueled by AI, presents an exciting future full of unleashed innovation, creativity and imagination.

title: Council Post: Rethinking AI In The Context Of Sustainability
text:
Guy F. Courtin - Vice President of Industry and Global Alliances, Tecsys.
Large language models (LLMs), natural language processing (NLP), machine learning (ML), cognitive AI and a litany of other “hot” artificial intelligence technologies have flooded our discussions since early 2023. From media coverage to overzealous CEOs, the message ringing in our ears is clear—get on the AI train or be left behind.
From helping solve your supply chain planning problems and enhancing customer service to improving patient care, determining better product mixes and reducing the number of HR memos, AI has been bellowed from the rooftops as the next elixir to all our ills. There’s no doubt that AI holds great opportunities for businesses and society but at what cost? And how does it impact another hot topic—sustainability?
A Hidden Conflict?
How soon we forget. Environmental, social and governance (ESG) responsibility—or sustainability—was once the subject of every headline. It was deemed a vital business driver and commanded above-the-fold ink not that long ago. However, being more sustainable remains an elusive target. Companies across all industries are striving to better understand, control and reach sustainable levels. Providing more transparency and reporting on ESG will soon become a requirement for publicly traded companies.
Is there a conflict between these two trends? Potentially. By some accounts, the environmental footprint needed to train OpenAI’s GPT-3 was the equivalent of “driving a car to the moon and back”—480,000 miles—and evaporating 700,000 liters of freshwater. Amplify that by the number of queries that are being pumped through LLMs like ChatGPT and the necessary computation power needed and the ecological toll becomes clear. However, there’s a fine line that companies can walk to leverage AI and still uphold their ESG commitments. Here’s what companies need to consider when it comes to ensuring AI efforts don’t conflict with ESG goals.
Aligning ESG And AI Strategies
Avoid the temptation to blindly rush into all things AI. There’s no question that AI’s impact continues to show remarkable promise, especially in the supply chain industry. Although there are clear AI use cases like demand forecasting, fascinating AI applications are emerging that extend into fulfillment, sourcing, warehousing and all aspects of logistics. However, that doesn’t mean companies should indeterminately chase every alluring and ambitious AI concept.
It’s essential to weigh the value of AI within specific scenarios. Consider the environmental footprint AI might have in much the same way you would assess the caloric content and nutritional value of the foods in your diet. Being thoughtful about when to deploy AI means embracing the discipline of rigorously analyzing each potential application and balancing the effort and resources required for AI against the expected benefits. Does the computation power needed justify the ecological impact? Are the savings or commercial advantages gained through AI deployment proportional to its sustainability costs? This conscientious approach ensures that your AI strategy isn’t only aligned with immediate business objectives but also resonates with your ESG mandate.
If you haven’t already, begin to craft and implement an ESG strategy. McKinsey researchers point out that companies must determine which part of “ESG” is most relevant to their business and, by extension, their supply chains. In their report, McKinsey researchers provide examples like “a multinational pharmaceutical company may focus on social metrics (such as accessibility and affordability)” while “a food company may elevate an equal mix of environmental (emissions reductions, water use, and waste) and social metrics (nutrition, product quality, and safety).” Building on this, forward-thinking companies must include AI usage when thinking of the “E” in ESG. Determine how influential that aspect is to your ESG strategy and weigh the impact of increased AI usage.
For any of these policies to effect meaningful change, they must be communicated across your entire network. It’s vital to communicate clearly how you’re approaching ESG and AI and that key stakeholders grasp the importance of adhering to those standards. Look to leading companies like Schneider Electric, FedEx, Columbia Sportswear and Coca-Cola. These companies exemplify how to lead from the front and work with their network partners to enhance ESG compliance, including AI considerations.
Schneider Electric initiated a 2040 carbon-neutral target across its value chain. They did so by working with their top suppliers to map out their carbon footprints. Although interest from the suppliers was tepid at first, it’s grown to over 1,000 suppliers committing to the program. This was only possible because Schneider Electric took the lead, leaning on third parties to help map the suppliers’ carbon footprint. The result is a great example of an organization working with its network to address this issue.
Looking at how AI will impact your ESG efforts has to become part of the conversation because AI isn’t going away. It will only expand as more use cases are being put through the AI machine. At the same time, the importance of sustainable practices and ESG compliance continues to grow, both for organizational integrity and for our planet. Companies must be savvier and more conscious when it comes to how, where and to what extent their AI initiatives will shape their future. It’s essential to remember that although AI is an incredibly potent tool, it carries inherent environmental implications. Balancing AI’s capabilities with responsible, sustainable practices isn’t just beneficial but necessary for true progress.

title: AI is Uncle Sam’s new secret weapon to fight fraud | CNN Business
text: Uncle Sam has quietly deployed a new secret weapon designed to catch bad guys trying to steal from taxpayers: artificial intelligence. Starting around late 2022, the Treasury Department began using enhanced fraud-detection methods powered by AI to spot fraud, CNN has learned. The strategy mirrors what is already being done in the private sector. Banks and payment companies are increasingly turning to AI to root out suspicious transactions – which the technology can often do with lightning speed. Uncle Sam’s AI-fueled crackdown on fraud appears to be paying off. Treasury’s AI-powered fraud detection recovered $375 million in fiscal 2023 alone, Treasury officials tell CNN, marking the first time Treasury is publicly acknowledging it is using AI to detect fraud. The federal government, using these new crime-fighting strategies, can halt check fraud almost in real-time in part by looking for unusual transaction patterns, Treasury officials tell CNN. And this focus on AI has led to multiple active cases and arrests by law enforcement, Treasury says. Treasury is not relying on generative AI, the technology powering ChatGPT and other popular tools that can create song lyrics, conjure up images and even create movie-quality videos from text prompts. Instead, Treasury officials say the type of AI they are using falls more into the bucket of machine learning and Big Data. The goal is to move with such speed that anomalies are flagged and banks are alerted before fraudulent checks are ever cashed, Treasury officials said. Fraud spiked after Covid Washington needs all the help it can get on the fraud front. Fraud spiked during the Covid-19 pandemic. US officials were under enormous pressure in 2020 and 2021 to quickly distribute aid to families and small businesses devastated by the health crisis. Fraudsters took advantage of the unprecedented flow of money from Washington. As much as $135 billion in fraudulent Covid unemployment insurance claims were likely paid out by states, according to the US Government Accountability Office. The Small Business Administration may have distributed more than $200 billion in fraudulent Covid funds. Check fraud has surged by 385% since the pandemic, according to Treasury. The number of suspicious activity reports (SARs) filed by financial institutions nearly doubled in 2022 to more than 680,000, according to Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN). This is a particular problem for Treasury, which is among the biggest payers on the planet – if not the biggest. Last year alone Treasury dispersed 1.4 billion payments totaling $6.9 trillion, covering everything from Social Security payments to tax refunds. “We are using the latest technological advances to enhance our fraud-detection process, and AI has allowed us to expedite the detection of fraud and recovery of tax dollars,” Deputy Treasury Secretary Wally Adeyemo said in a statement provided to CNN. News of Treasury’s use of AI comes after the Internal Revenue Service announced last September it started deploying AI to detect tax cheats. The IRS said its experts will apply “cutting-edge machine learning technology” to examine large and complex partnership tax returns – including those of hedge funds, law firms and real estate investment firms. Catching fraud in milliseconds Amiram Shachar, co-founder and CEO of cloud security startup Upwind, told CNN the federal government should “absolutely” use AI to detect fraud. “AI can help humans operate more efficiently, allowing them to see more in shorter timeframes,” said Shachar. “This is especially important in the government, where there are headcount constraints. They can’t compete with Google and Facebook for the best talent.” Shachar, whose firm recently raised funding from Penny Jar Capital, a venture firm backed by NBA superstar Steph Curry, said financial institutions are using AI to verify all major areas of transactions almost in real-time. “Once you train a model, the speed you can catch things is in milliseconds. It’s incredible,” he said. Could AI turbocharge fraud? As AI continues to evolve, the private sector is experimenting with how the technology can be used to root out fraud. Earlier this month, Mastercard announced it built an advanced generative AI model aimed at helping banks determine whether transactions are legitimate. The payments giant said the new AI technology will be able to scan an unprecedented one trillion data points, boosting fraud-detection rates by an average of 20% and perhaps by as much as 300% in some cases. Even as the public and private sectors turn to AI to fight crime, US officials are increasingly concerned over the risks the technology poses to the financial system. Late last year, the Financial Stability Oversight Council, a team of leading regulators led by the Treasury secretary, for the first time formally classified AI as an “emerging vulnerability.” Experts are especially worried about how AI can turbocharge financial fraud. Earlier this month, a finance worker at a company was duped into paying out $25 million to fraudsters. In the elaborate scheme, Hong Kong police say the worker was tricked into thinking they were participating in a legitimate video call that was actually a deepfake video.

title: Council Post: Fleet Technology In 2024: A Look At The Year Ahead
text:
Aarjav Trivedi is the founder and CEO of Ridecell, a leading intelligent automation platform for fleets.
When it comes to fleets, change is afoot on several fronts, centering around shared mobility, electric vehicles (EVs) and artificial intelligence (AI). Based on my observations and experience with fleet automation platforms, let's take a closer look at the trends in each of these areas to home in on the ways that fleets will be deployed in the year ahead.
1. Shared mobility will shift to B2B—especially because of ESG.
There’s a growing sense that shared mobility has entered the trough of disillusionment—and it’s certainly not hard to find reasons to be gloomy if you’re looking at the B2C instances of shared mobility. But B2B is a different story. And in the coming year, I believe the center of gravity for shared mobility will shift to B2B.
One of the reasons why B2B is fertile ground for shared mobility is because it is an effective way for corporations to meet their sustainability goals. For instance, even if only 10% of your company’s vehicle fleet is EVs, you can use keyless and sharing technologies and automation to prioritize the usage of those vehicles so that the EVs get the highest utilization rates. As a result, you can have the majority of your total vehicle miles accomplished via EVs, even if those EVs only comprise 10% of the fleet. That’s a powerful “force multiplier” for sustainability efforts.
2. Acquiring EVs is good, but effectively managing them is better.
The above raises an important point, which is that while prioritizing usage of EVs and ensuring they get high utilization is a valuable activity, making it happen isn’t easy. That’s because as EVs become more prominent in fleets, companies need to be able to match vehicles to specific use cases, depending upon the state of charge of the EV’s battery.
For example, does a city employee need to run a 20-minute errand and pick up some paperwork from the other side of town, or do they need to drive 100 miles to the state capital and file some paperwork? State of charge matters here, and an EV with only a partial charge would only be suitable for one of those scenarios. Likewise, a delivery fleet needs the ability to match a delivery vehicle charge to the route as opposed to keeping the same driver in the same vehicle daily.
What this example demonstrates is that acquiring EVs is only the first step toward a more effective fleet operation; there needs to be some supporting workflows wrapped around those EVs in order for companies to not just maintain them and keep them charged but also assign a driver to a car that has the proper level of charge for whatever routine they’re carrying out.
For the most part, these workflows—whether it’s scheduling a car to come in for routine maintenance or assigning a specific driver to a specific vehicle—are carried out manually today. The routine and repeatable nature of these tasks, however, makes them strong candidates for automation. In the coming year, I believe many companies will likely shift their attention from the acquisition of EV and infrastructure deployments to finding ways to scale that infrastructure through automation. Steps like these can help your company make the most of the EVs you have.
3. AI is ascendant—but why train someone else’s AI with your data?
No discussion of the brave new world that will unfold over the coming months is complete without a mention of AI. Simply put, fleets are becoming increasingly immersed in the stuff.
An early use case for AI in the fleet space was predictive maintenance. But it doesn’t stop there; cabin monitoring systems can use AI to more accurately determine distracted driving, onset of fatigue or smoking of prohibited substances by their drivers. Meanwhile, the front-facing cameras in vehicles capture enough data that AI can analyze it and use it for accident reconstruction to accurately determine who was at fault in a fender-bender—and to decide whether they need to take someone to court or start settling ASAP.
The list goes on. Most (if not all) fleet management tools can benefit from AI, so expect vendors to increasingly fold this technology into their offerings. In taking advantage of these tools, however, companies will essentially be training someone else’s AI with their data. I don't think it will be very long before a handful of companies realize that they’re giving away valuable training data and instead try to harness it in-house to develop and train their own AI models.
One way to start this process is by interconnecting different fleet management systems to break down standalone data silos. After all, you can’t create a very smart AI model unless you have access to a rich sweep of data. It's certainly possible to collect data individually from each silo, but this is typically more time-consuming and potentially more error-prone. If your business takes this approach, be mindful to pay special attention to the different file formats and naming conventions used by the different systems as you merge and reconcile data.
Regardless of which approach they utilize to bring data together, I believe those companies that make the effort in this regard will be well-rewarded and will find themselves with a competitive advantage over those that don’t.
The Common Denominator For Success
What do all these developments have in common? It’s that embracing digital transformation and automating various aspects of fleet operations can give you the upper hand in the year to come, whether that means making better usage of EVs and tackling ESG goals or more fully tapping into the power of AI. Ultimately, seek to navigate these areas with an eye on innovation and transformation—and stay ahead of the curve.

title: Council Post: CX Trends Dominating The Industry Today
text:
Global marketing leader at HGS, CX professional, product promoter, outsourcing innovation fan – with a focus on what’s next.
As a communications executive in 2024, finding the right balance of advanced technology and skilled talent for your desired brand experience is a top priority. Upholding a customer-centric approach, exploiting AI's potential and ensuring consistency while innovating and fostering cross-functional collaboration are the pillars of successful customer experience (CX) strategies.
To help brands plot robust CX strategies, my company commissioned a survey of CX decision-makers in the United States to gain data-driven insights and identify technology deployment priorities for the next 18 months. Before our survey, we found the industry needed a fresh look at CX buyer dynamics data and broader information representing a larger scope of financial implications, AI and decision dynamics.
We surveyed 300 U.S. CX decision-makers in roles from executive director to chair member between August 29 and September 10, 2023. As the global head of marketing and executive vice president, I will break down these insights to present CX industry trends and outline the critical areas where leaders should direct their strategies in 2024.
A Customer-Centric Mindset Dominates The Industry
More than ever, organizations recognize the importance of adopting a customer-centric culture. According to the CX Buyers' Insights report, more than 3 in 5 CX decision-makers (63%) emphasize adopting a customer-centric organizational culture as the most important factor for maintaining a competitive edge in customer care innovation.
Furthermore, providing a seamless experience across various channels—including physical stores, websites, mobile apps, social media and customer support—is crucial. Customers expect to switch between channels effortlessly and have consistent interactions, influenced by the expectations set by digital giants like Amazon, Apple and Google. Here are some focus areas for brands to meet customers’ new expectations:
• Personalized Messages: Implement personalized marketing campaigns, product recommendations and communication based on customer data insights.
• Responsive Customer Service: Develop agile processes and stay updated on industry trends to proactively adjust strategies and synchronize with customer preferences.
• Employee Training and Engagement: Train employees to effectively execute a personalized approach and foster a customer-centric culture that aligns all team members to provide an excellent CX.
Balance AI and Human Interactions With More Consistent Training
In pursuing an enhanced CX, organizations are placing significant bets on AI. A staggering 58% of businesses plan to invest in new AI technologies to automate customer interactions, according to the report.
While AI and automation are instrumental in streamlining processes, live human interactions remain essential in providing a positive CX. Customer care teams serve as brand champions, and people should be the focal point of an organization’s CX strategy and beneficiaries of the implementation of AI augmentation, as they bring customers’ interactions with the brand to life.
Therefore, effective and continuous agent enablement and training—designated as one of the cornerstones for success—is prioritized by 61% of CX decision-makers. The ongoing commitment to updating training programs with AI tools ensures that customer care agents are adequately equipped to navigate intricate challenges.
This focus on training not only contributes to the seamless integration of AI and human interactions but also addresses sentiments of inequity or frustration, fortifying the overall CX.
Leveraging training simulations driven by large language models, which draw insights from millions of past customer interactions, can empower organizations to properly prepare human support for any scenario. It allows them to brainstorm improved strategies for leading with automation, integrating people into the process in a manner perceived as a value addition, rather than mere escalation in instances when the bot encounters challenges.
While training simulations are crucial, companies must also focus on internal initiatives to balance AI and human interactions. Fostering a culture of continuous learning is key, with training sessions on AI integration for CX teams to bridge knowledge gaps and receive personalized feedback. Mentorship programs also enhance team adaptability, creating an environment that values technological proficiencies and human-centric skills.
This multifaceted approach ensures organizations manage customer needs while maximizing AI’s potential.
Leaders Find Collaboration Key To Keeping Up
Collaboration emerges as a key theme to maintain a competitive edge in customer care innovation. Over half of CX decision-makers (54%) identify collaborating with industry partners as a top factor in building a strong, cost-effective approach to CX.
Strategic partnerships not only diversify contact center operations geographically but also optimize service availability around the clock, offer access to scalable talent and drive cost savings. In the dynamic CX environment, collaboration with industry partners is a strategic imperative for navigating the evolving landscape of innovation with foresight and efficiency.
For companies looking for a great CX partner, here’s a checklist to guide your journey:
• Define clear objectives.
• Thoroughly research potential partners.
• Prioritize collaborative compatibility.
• Seek experienced partners with a proven track record.
Once a partnership is established, the CX partner must understand client objectives, provide regular updates and proactively solve problems. CX partnerships often struggle due to communication gaps, misaligned goals and resistance to change. To overcome these challenges, prioritize transparent communication and foster adaptability.
Conclusion
Businesses must stay informed on CX trends to maintain a competitive edge. As AI advances, it's not just about smarter technology, but how it redefines our customer engagement. Predictive analytics, powered by AI, can help to anticipate needs, ensuring every interaction is as unique as the customer.
For example, in the realm of customer service, AI can predict when a customer might face an issue and automatically dispatch proactive solutions, perhaps even before the customer is aware of the issue. For sales and marketing, AI analyzes a customer’s purchase history to suggest new products tailored to their preferences. In both cases, the technology blends seamlessly with human expertise to create a CX that’s both efficient and personal.
The future is collaborative; AI will enhance human roles, not replace them, elevating our strategic capabilities in delivering superior experiences. It's an exciting horizon where AI, partners and customers play critical roles in the evolution of CX.

title: Council Post: Speaking The Same Language: How Advances In NLP Can Uncover Insights And Enable Proper Guidance
text:
CEO and Cofounder of AnswerRocket.
The combination of large language models (LLMs) and modern analytics technology—along with advances in natural language processing (NLP)—are empowering ordinary business users to unlock critical insights and guidance from their organization's massive collection of data. This is having a significant impact on enterprises: Not only can they make better decisions, but they can make them faster since they don't have to rely on the manual, byzantine analytics workflows of yesteryear.
Evolving From SQL Queries To Rigid NLP To LLM-Powered Conversational NLP
In the past, analysts had to execute SQL queries to analyze their business data. When it came to advanced data analysis, this often required engaging data scientists to develop purpose-built machine learning models.
This, of course, was a cumbersome process that made it difficult for laypeople to analyze and glean insights from their data. Thus, business users were heavily reliant on their more technical colleagues to field their analytics requests—often creating bottlenecks for these critical insights and limiting broader data-driven decision-making.
NLP technology aimed to improve this experience and make data analysis more accessible to business users with the promise of eliminating the need for SQL know-how. At this point, you could just ask a question in plain words to get an answer. Until recently, however, this approach was still rigid. Users needed to know about the underlying data.
For example, the system wouldn't automatically know that sales are the same as revenue unless those synonyms were established. There was still a precise way you had to ask questions to get accurate insights. Metric by dimension by time period questions worked well ("What were sales by category in 2023?"), but more humanistic questions failed ("What was my sales trend by category?"). This learning curve of having to understand how the data is structured and how to formulate a successful query was difficult for many users to overcome.
Over the past year or so, LLMs have completely flipped the script. Now, it's actually feasible for users to ask business questions in their own words and quickly get a data-driven answer.
Improvements in NLP in the age of LLMs have taken conversational analytics further and are pushing the bounds of what's possible with generative AI. With these advancements, users can speak in their own terms. They can talk to their data just like they would to a human or a colleague. For example, they can ask something like, "Hey, what’s going on with sales? Why are they dipping?" Before LLMs, analytics platforms would not have understood that sort of colloquial language.
It's important to reiterate that this means far more than just moving from an SQL query to asking what sales were last year. As referenced above, that is still a rules-based and very rigid process. These advancements make analytics even more accessible, enabling general users who struggled with natural language analytics platforms before to easily use the technology.
Now, these users don't have to think about how to ask questions or worry about crafting the perfect prompt. Instead of humans having to adapt and learn the technology, NLP has finally adapted to users, allowing them to ask questions naturally.
Beyond Data Insights: The Rise Of Recommendations
This transformation has also done more than just democratize data insights; it's given users powerful recommendations. Coupled with machine learning-powered data analytics, NLP gains deeper intelligence and more capacity for answering nuanced questions ("How are sales doing?") as well as advising users on what will happen, what they should do now or how they should allocate their marketing budgets.
In short, people are moving from being told "what" to being told "now what?" This is a seismic shift from descriptive statistics to predictive analytics and prescriptive actions.
There's one quick bit of caution. To get good guidance, users need to make sure they're leveraging specialized LLM copilots that are tailored to their business, industry and goals. This could be a copilot designed by a vendor or a custom copilot created by a developer within the organization. However, the bottom line is it needs to be purpose-built for what you do and rooted in a solid understanding of your domain.
Broadly speaking, LLMs are designed to give you feedback when you feed them a prompt even if they don't have the right answers. A general copilot will give you a recommendation even though it doesn't understand your business. You can ask the public version of ChatGPT anything ("What should I do with my budget?"), and it'll respond. However, it will be a generic answer that you likely can't trust.
Make sure you're only taking guidance from qualified generative AI technologies.
Continuing NLP Advancements Will Unlock More From Data
LLMs have made analytics easier and more impactful than ever before. The full potential is only just now unfolding. Continued NLP innovation will enable organizations and users to do more and better things with their data.
We're moving toward a future where virtually every member of an organization—regardless of their technical abilities—can effectively tap into data to drive their decision-making. The impact on business intelligence and analytics adoption will be profound, unlocking a path toward more innovative and transformative business strategies.

title: What White-Collar Jobs Are Safe From AI—And Which Professions Are Most At Risk?
text:
The accelerated ascendancy of artificial intelligence has created a booming new tech sector offering plentiful opportunities for growth. Understandably, there are grave concerns about how this fast-emerging technology will impact the job market. Most notably, white-collar workers are fearful that they may be made redundant, as AI poses a threat to their job security.
Like robotics impressed upon the blue-collar labor market, in factories and warehouses, “AI is on a collision course with white-collar, high-paid jobs,” CNBC reported.
“AI is distinguished from past technologies that have come over the last 100-plus years,” said Rakesh Kochhar, a senior researcher at Pew Research Center. “It is reaching up from the factory floors into the office spaces where white-collar, higher-paid workers tend to be.”
Investment bank Goldman Sachs predicted in a 2023 report that the workforce in the United States and Europe would be upended, with 300 million jobs lost or diminished by this fast-growing technology.
In a recent survey conducted by ResumeBuilder, 37% of business leaders revealed they have already begun to replace staff with AI. Nearly half (44%) of the executive respondents stated they anticipate further jobs cuts in 2024 due to AI efficiency.
Several employers have already enacted headcount reductions this year. Additionally, it looks like they plan to reallocate the money saved from downsizing toward investments into AI, machine learning, automation and bringing aboard experienced professionals in this space. The redirection of funds and resources to this fast-emerging technology adds another layer of job risk for white-collar workers.
White-Collar Jobs That Are Less Likely To Be Impacted By AI
Roles that require a significant social or emotional component are less susceptible to automation due to the human element involved, such as therapists, counselors, social workers and teachers. Additionally, high-level white-collar workers that are responsible for making complex business decisions are less likely to be displaced by AI. Customer-facing positions, such as salespeople who need to engage and build relationships with clients, are safe from being made obsolete by this technology.
Management consultants who spend their time negotiating project terms, understanding client needs and providing strategic advice require a high degree of human interaction and problem-solving, have futureproofed careers.
Lawyers spend a good deal of their time arguing their cases in court and negotiating settlements, which require the human touch. Although attorneys may seem completely immune, AI can now review legal documents more efficiently and are less likely to be subject to human error
At first blush, roles that involve a high degree of human creativity may seem above reproach. Unfortunately, for the creative professionals, AI can generate high-quality art, videos and designs, which poses a threat to these jobs.
While some components of human resources can be completed by AI, including employment contracts, offer letters, payroll, benefits and engagement surveys, others cannot. Resolving conflicts and managing employee relations require a high level of interpersonal skills and understanding of human behavior, and will continue to need a human involved with the process.
The Most Vulnerable and Impacted Professions
Roles focused on data analysis, bookkeeping, basic financial reporting and repetitive administrative tasks are highly susceptible to automation.
Jobs involving rote processes, scheduling and basic customer service are increasingly handled by AI. AI-powered writing tools are impacting media and marketing, in addition to drafting legal documents. Customer service inquiries are being supplanted by chatbots and AI-powered assistants.
Slow-Walking Hiring Waiting for the AI Takeover?
Some companies may delay hiring due to economic uncertainty or strategic business transformations. The slow-moving nature of the job market suggests that companies are taking a wait-and-see approach when it comes to AI.
Businesses may be dragging their feet to hire people, as they feel that AI could take over many tasks that a white-collar office worker could do.
In an earnings call last month, Alphabet CFO Ruth Porat said the company is exhibiting a “slower pace of hiring.” When discussing how Microsoft is able to make margin improvements, CFO Amy Hood told investors the company is “re-pivoting our workforce toward the AI-first work we're doing, without adding material number of people to the workforce.”
Technology has always been a way to bring down cost relative to the compensation offered to highly paid workers. It seems unlikely that AI will fully replace white-collar jobs in the next few years. Also, AI isn’t a cure-all for everything work related. While it can automate specific tasks, there is still a need for human skills, such as critical thinking, creativity, emotional intelligence and social interactions.
It is more likely that AI will augment and enhance human capabilities rather than replace them entirely. Workers who adapt and utilize AI tools effectively will have the upper hand.
If You’re Worried, Try Reskilling and Upskilling
How susceptible is your specific role to automation? Are there opportunities available within your industry to transition to a less AI-impacted niche? Do you have transferable skills that you can leverage in different fields?
Research alternative career paths by exploring industries and roles that align with your interests and skills. Connect with people in your target field to gain insights and build your network.
Continuous learning and acquiring new skills will be crucial for navigating the changing job market. Many online platforms offer courses, certifications and training programs to develop new skills.
To maximize your employability, you can choose to go where there is a growing need in the market. Although there is a lot of discussion about how AI will take jobs, the technology will also create new roles. New and emerging roles in the workforce include:
- AI specialists and developers
- Data scientists and analysts with domain expertise
- User experience and human-computer interaction specialists
- Creative professionals who can collaborate with AI tools.
- AI Ethics Officer
- Data privacy specialist
- AI-assisted healthcare provider
- AI implementation strategist
Become The Best At What You Do
In addition to bridging any skills gaps, you want to be perceived as the best at what you do. It is mission-critical to stand out among your peers and make yourself irreplaceable. You want to develop a personal brand and carve out a niche that positions you as a leading expert in your space. AI is never going to supersede the expertise and influence held by well respected industry leaders.

title: Premarket stocks: Revolution or market bubble? Investors weigh the AI boom | CNN Business
text: A version of this story first appeared in CNN Business’ Before the Bell newsletter. Not a subscriber? You can sign up right here. You can listen to an audio version of the newsletter by clicking the same link. What’s the difference between a revolution and a market bubble? Often, it’s time and patience — two things that Wall Street is notoriously lacking. But as the artificial intelligence boom reaches into more areas of workers’ lives and sends stocks hurtling sky high, some investors worry about whether AI is the real deal and what happens if it isn’t. What’s happening: Shares of Nvidia have exploded higher with no end to their upward trajectory in sight. The California chipmaker’s stock is about 240% higher over the past year, and it isn’t alone. AMD is up 126.5% since a year ago, and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co stock is nearly 50% higher over the same period. The so-called Magnificent Seven tech stocks — Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, Amazon, Google, Meta and Tesla — that dominate the S&P 500 have also benefited greatly from AI buzz. They’re collectively up about 55% over the past year. Large companies, meanwhile, are already shifting their resources to invest heavily in AI technology and are sometimes laying off employees in anticipation of an increase in productivity through automation. “This is not hype,” JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon told CNBC on Monday of AI. Dimon, who is often skeptical of new technologies and fads, said that there are about 200 people at JPMorgan dedicated to researching generative AI. “When we had the internet bubble the first time around… that was hype. This is not hype. It’s real,” he said. “People are deploying it at different speeds, but it will handle a tremendous amount of stuff.” Not everyone is convinced: The top 10 companies in the S&P 500 are more overvalued today than they were during the tech bubble in the mid-1990s, wrote Torsten Slok, chief economist at Apollo Global Management, in a note to investors on Sunday, citing the companies’ price to earnings ratios. The growth of these companies has created a Teflon stock market — nothing bad seems to stick to it, even higher-than-expected inflation data and delayed expectations for interest rate cuts by the Federal Reserve, said Yung-Yu Ma, chief investment officer at BMO Wealth Management. “The idea that AI can unleash both spending and productivity is a strong narrative that markets are focused on right now,” he said. But that sole focus on AI is worrisome. “Thoughts of the mid-1990s (tech boom) are creeping into today’s equity market, as during that time the ensuing productivity boom propelled equities for years despite relatively high interest rates,” he said. “The current hype may be slightly more advanced than what AI can deliver in the near-term for productivity gains.” Looking under the hood: Some shareholders are also worried about Big Tech’s investment in AI. Apple is reportedly on track to spend $1 billion a year on generative AI. Two very large Apple investors, Norges Bank Investment Management and Legal & General, have said that they will support a resolution at the company’s annual shareholder meeting Wednesday that would require the iPhone maker to disclose and report AI-related risks. The proposal asks the company to “disclose any ethical guidelines that the company has adopted regarding use of AI technology.” The shareholder proposal was introduced by the union federation AFL-CIO. In a filing to the US Securities and Exchange Commission, Apple proposed the vote be skipped. Lawyers for the company argued that shareholders were being too controlling by requesting the disclosure of AI risks. The SEC disagreed. “In our view, the proposal transcends ordinary business matters and does not seek to micromanage the company,” the agency wrote. Number of 401(k) ‘millionaires’ jumped 41% last year, says Fidelity Many more new 401(k) “millionaires” were created last year, but the overall number remains low, according to data released Tuesday. Thanks to strong performances in stocks and bonds in 2023, coupled with steady savings rates and employer-provided matching contributions, 401(k) investors ended 2023 very much in the black, reports my colleague Jeanne Sahadi. That’s according to new fourth-quarter data from Fidelity Investments, one of the largest providers of workplace retirement plans that cover 23 million 401(k) participants. The average 401(k) balance rose to $118,600 at the end of the fourth quarter, up 14% for the year. Among Gen Xers, the demographic cohort that will start retiring over the next decade, Fidelity found that the average 401(k) balance topped $500,000 among those who have been saving for at least 15 years consecutively. Fidelity also reported that the number of 401(k) accounts with balances of at least $1 million rose in the fourth quarter by 20%, to 422,000 accounts; and by 41% for the whole year. The average account balance for this group was $1,551,300 in the fourth quarter. But market performance isn’t the only factor to credit for higher balances. Actual savings habits played a big role. Fidelity said that 27% of plan participants proactively increased their contribution rate throughout last year. And 78% of 401(k) savers were contributing at a rate high enough to get their employer’s full matching contribution. Between employee and employer contributions, the average savings rate last year was 13.9%, up slightly from 13.7% a year earlier. Beyond Meat’s stock surges after CEO promises to steeply cut costs in 2024 Shares of Beyond Meat skyrocketed in after-hours trading on Tuesday after the company promised to cut costs and transition to a “leaner operating structure” in its fourth-quarter financial report. The troubled plant-based meat company, which has partnerships with McDonald’s and KFC owner Yum! Brands, has faced falling demand for its products and ballooning costs in recent years. But on Tuesday, the company announced a turnaround plan, reports my colleague Samantha Delouya. “Our 2024 plan includes taking steps to steeply reduce operating expense and cash use,” Beyond Meat CEO Ethan Brown said in a statement. Overall, Beyond Meat reported a 7.8% decrease in year-over-year net revenues to $73.7 million, beating Wall Street’s expectations for the quarter, according to Factset. The report sent shares of Beyond Meat surging. The stock was up more than 70% in after-hours trading on Tuesday after falling more than 60% in the past year. On a Tuesday call with Beyond Meat’s investors, Brown outlined a set of initiatives intended to rightsize the struggling company. Brown said the company would cut at least $70 million from Beyond Meat’s operating budget in 2024. As part of those cuts, Brown said, Beyond Meat would “tighten” its focus and trim some of its offerings, discontinuing its Beyond Meat jerky line. Brown said the discontinuation would allow the company to put its resources toward other products “which we believe have higher profitable growth potential.” Beyond Meat did not specify whether it may conduct layoffs as part of its cost-cutting measures.
